reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents an Ethereum bot as an easy daily passive-income opportunity and directs viewers to fund a specific contract with at least 0.5 ETH. It claims that supplying more ETH can produce more profit, while reported rapid gains and withdrawal of the deposit plus profit reinforce the promoted monetary return. The records do not independently verify the bot, code, displayed balance, transfer, or claimed outcome.

citations.quote: Today I'll be teaching you step by step how to deploy an Ethereum trading bot I've recently. Developed in the Solidity language, which can make you very easy daily passive income.
7)Deposit funds (at least 0.5 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
Obviously the more you put in, the larger the transactions you will be able to. Sandwich, and the more profit you'll be able to accumulate over time.
Last step is to click start. This will enable the bot to start sniffing the mempool to find different liquidity pairs. In order for you to sandwich transactions.
I have about 1.31 Ethereum which is 31% profit already.

opening.argument: Judge, the funding amount is presented as a way to account for costs, not as a threshold that guarantees returns. The description warns that fees can exceed profit when the contract is underfunded, and the speaker says profits fluctuate. Those qualifications matter when assessing whether the video promises effortless, certain income. The claims about results deserve scrutiny, but the stated possibility of losing money to fees supports reading this as a risky trading-tool tutorial rather than a guaranteed-return offer.

citations.quote: If you fund the contract with 0.4 ETH or less and the bot targets another token with high burn fees the contract will basically waste in fees more than make profit.
The profits will fluctuate week to week.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening cites a funding recommendation and a reported gain, but neither establishes a guaranteed payout. Its treatment of 0.5 ETH as a profit trigger omits the stated reason for that amount: avoiding losses to fees. The speaker's reported 31% gain is a claim about one run, while the same account expressly says results vary.

citations.quote: I recommend funding the contract with around 0.5 - 1 ETH just to make sure that won't happen.
The profits will fluctuate week to week.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A warning about fees does not undo the pitch. Viewers are told to deposit at least 0.5 ETH, start the bot, and expect profit from the funded contract. The speaker then reports rapid gains and describes returning the initial ETH plus profit. Uncertainty about the exact return does not make the solicitation merely educational.

citations.quote: 7)Deposit funds (at least 0.5 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
When you click withdraw the bot will exit the liquidity pool and return the total Ethereum. You entered initially including the profit back to your wallet.

opening.argument: Judge, the central sequence is an operational walkthrough: create a contract file, paste source code, select a compiler version, deploy through a wallet provider, and inspect the resulting contract. The speaker also explains the proposed transaction mechanism. That instructional detail gives a reason to read the reported balance as part of a demonstration, not as proof of what any viewer will earn. The record cannot independently validate the bot or the result, but lack of validation alone does not erase the tutorial's technical focus.

citations.quote: 3)Right click on the 'contracts' folder and create a new file. Rename it as you like—i.e., 'Bot.sol'
5)Move to the 'Solidity Compiler' tab, select version '0.6.6' and then click 'Compile'
It takes advantage of decentralized finance platforms such as Uniswap to sandwich transactions. For arbitrage.
So let's copy the smart contract address to. Make sure it's created. I'm gonna head back over to Etherscan and paste it in.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening is right that the speaker reports easy income and a 31% gain. But those statements occur within a narrated deployment and test, not in isolation. The quoted instruction to fund the contract is one step in that workflow; it does not, by itself, verify that the reported result was fabricated or that the linked code diverts funds.

citations.quote: Next, if you look in the description, I've included a link to the bot's source code. You're going to want to copy this code and paste it into the file bot.sol you've just. Created.
So the next step is to fund the contract with. Some Ethereum to snipe liquidity pools.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The walkthrough is precisely how viewers are led into the funded workflow. After the deployment steps, the speaker tells them to send ETH to the contract and activate the bot, then presents a large return as the result. Showing compiler and wallet controls does not verify that the supplied code performs the claimed trading or that viewers can recover their deposits.

citations.quote: That means it was sent to the contract. We can make sure by checking our contract address on etherscan once again, making sure. Our ethereum is in the contract.
Last step is to click start. This will enable the bot to start sniffing the mempool to find different liquidity pairs.
So as you can see I have about 1.31 Ethereum which is 31% profit already.

opening.argument: Judge, this can be read as promotion of a deployable software tool. The instructions say the viewer deploys the contract through their wallet and funds the resulting contract address; they do not show a payment to the speaker, a credential handover, or income from recruiting others. The speaker describes a withdrawal control, though that description is not proof it works. A funding step and an ambitious earnings claim warrant caution, but the supplied record does not establish where the deposited ETH ultimately goes or demonstrate that a third party takes it.

citations.quote: 'Injected Web3' as the environment, then click 'Deploy'. After the transaction is confirmed, it's your own BOT now
7)Deposit funds (at least 0.5 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
Withdraw anytime by clicking 'withdrawal'

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference opening identifies the strongest concern: viewers are urged to fund a contract in pursuit of returns. But its own evidentiary limitation matters. Without verification of the linked code or the transfers, the record does not show a recipient controlled by the speaker or prove that the withdrawal function fails. The described destination is the viewer's deployed contract address, so the funding instruction alone does not settle those questions.

citations.quote: After the transaction is confirmed, it's your own BOT now
7)Deposit funds (at least 0.5 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A demonstrated payment to the speaker is not necessary to recognize the promoted funded-contract returns scheme. The video supplies external code, tells viewers to deploy and fund it with substantial ETH, and connects a larger deposit to greater expected profit. Calling the deployed address 'your own' does not establish what the code does with funds or whether its withdrawal control works.
